lessons.title: OOP Concepts and Principles
lessons.overview: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm based on the concept of 'objects' that contain data (attributes) and code (methods). C++ supports OOP through classes, objects, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism. OOP makes code more modular, reusable, and easier to maintain.
keyConcepts: Class: A blueprint/template that defines the structure (data members) and behavior (member functions) of objects
Object: An instance of a class — a concrete entity created from the class blueprint
Encapsulation: Bundling data and methods together, hiding internal details using access specifiers (private, public, protected)
Inheritance: A class (child/derived) can inherit properties and methods from another class (parent/base), enabling code reuse
Polymorphism: Same interface, different behavior — achieved through function overloading, operator overloading, and virtual functions
Abstraction: Hiding complex implementation details and showing only essential features
Procedural vs OOP: Procedural focuses on functions and steps. OOP focuses on objects and their interactions.
formulas: Access specifiers: public (accessible anywhere), private (class only), protected (class + derived classes)
Class definition: class ClassName { access: members; };  (note the semicolon)
Object creation: ClassName obj; or ClassName obj(params);

tables.title: Procedural vs Object-Oriented Programming
tables.note: OOP provides better data security and code reuse than procedural programming.

codeExamples.title: Defining a Class and Creating Objects
codeExamples.explanation: The class Student has private data members (name, rollNo, marks) and public member functions (setData, display). Objects s1 and s2 are instances of Student, each with their own copy of the data.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the semicolon after the class definition: class Car { ... }; ← the ; is required
Accessing private members directly from outside the class — use public getter/setter functions instead
Not using access specifiers — by default, members in a class are private (unlike struct where they're public)
examTips: Always end a class definition with a semicolon: };
Remember the 4 pillars: Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, Abstraction
By default, class members are private. struct members are public.
Know the difference between class (blueprint) and object (instance)

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four pillars of OOP?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The four pillars are: Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction. Compilation is a process, not an OOP principle.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the default access specifier for members in a C++ class?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In C++, class members are private by default. In a struct, members are public by default. This is the key difference between class and struct in C++.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the concept of hiding internal implementation details called?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Encapsulation bundles data and methods together and hides internal details using access specifiers (private, protected). The user only sees the public interface.

lessons.title: Constructors and Destructors
lessons.overview: A constructor is a special member function that is automatically called when an object is created. It initializes the object's data members. A destructor is called automatically when an object is destroyed (goes out of scope). Constructors have the same name as the class; destructors have a ~ prefix.
keyConcepts: Constructor: same name as the class, no return type (not even void), called automatically when object is created
Default constructor: takes no parameters — initializes members with default values
Parameterized constructor: takes parameters to initialize members with specific values
Copy constructor: initializes an object by copying another object of the same class
Destructor: name starts with ~, called automatically when object is destroyed, used for cleanup (freeing memory, closing files)
Constructor overloading: multiple constructors with different parameter lists
Only ONE destructor per class — cannot be overloaded

tables.title: Constructor vs Destructor
tables.note: Both are called automatically — you never call them directly.

codeExamples.title: All Types of Constructors + Destructor
codeExamples.explanation: Three constructors are demonstrated. The destructor is called automatically when each object goes out of scope at the end of main(). Objects are destroyed in reverse order of creation (LIFO).

commonMistakes: Giving a constructor a return type (even void) — this makes it a regular function, not a constructor
Forgetting the ~ in the destructor name
Trying to call a constructor directly — it's called automatically
Not initializing all members in the constructor (uninitialized members have garbage values)
Confusing the copy constructor with the assignment operator (=)
examTips: Constructors have NO return type — not even void
Destructors are called in reverse order of construction (LIFO)
If you don't define any constructor, the compiler provides a default constructor
If you define a parameterized constructor, the compiler does NOT provide a default constructor
Know the three types: default, parameterized, copy

practiceQuestions.question: What is the name of a destructor for class 'Car'?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A destructor is named with a tilde (~) prefix followed by the class name: ~Car(). It takes no parameters and has no return type.

practiceQuestions.question: What happens if you define a parameterized constructor but no default constructor?
options: Compiler provides a default constructor automatically
You cannot create objects without parameters
Objects are created with null values
practiceQuestions.explanation: If you define any constructor, the compiler does NOT provide a default constructor. So you can only create objects using the parameterized constructor. To create objects without parameters, you must explicitly define a default constructor.

practiceQuestions.question: In what order are destructors called when multiple objects go out of scope?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Destructors are called in reverse order of construction (LIFO — Last In, First Out). If objects were created as r1, r2, r3, destructors are called as r3, r2, r1.

lessons.title: Inheritance — Code Reuse and Hierarchy
lessons.overview: Inheritance is a mechanism where a new class (derived/child class) acquires the properties and behaviors of an existing class (base/parent class). It enables code reuse, hierarchical classification, and extensibility. The derived class can add new members or override existing ones.
keyConcepts: Base class (parent): the class being inherited from
Derived class (child): the class that inherits from the base class
Single inheritance: one base class, one derived class
Multiple inheritance: a class inherits from multiple base classes
Multilevel inheritance: A → B → C (chain of inheritance)
Hierarchical inheritance: multiple classes inherit from one base class
Access modes: public inheritance (public members stay public), protected inheritance, private inheritance
The derived class has access to public and protected members of the base class, but NOT private members
formulas: Public inheritance: class Student : public Person { };
Constructor call order: Base constructor → Derived constructor
Destructor call order: Derived destructor → Base destructor

tables.title: Inheritance Access Modes
tables.note: Private members of the base class are NEVER directly accessible in the derived class, regardless of inheritance mode.

diagrams.title: Types of Inheritance
diagrams.content:
Single:        Multiple:        Multilevel:        Hierarchical:

  A              A   B              A                    A
  ↑              ↑                 ↓                  ↙   ↘
  B              B                 B                  B     C
                                   ↑
                                   C

A = Base class, B/C = Derived class

codeExamples.title: Single Inheritance — Person → Student
codeExamples.explanation: Student inherits from Person. It can access the protected members (name, age) and public methods (setPerson, displayPerson) of Person. Student adds its own members (rollNo, marks) and methods (setStudent, displayStudent).

commonMistakes: Forgetting the access mode: class B : A defaults to private inheritance in C++
Trying to access private members of the base class directly — use protected instead
Forgetting to call the base class constructor in the derived class constructor's initializer list
examTips: Use 'protected' for members that should be accessible in derived classes but not outside
Constructor order: Base first, then Derived. Destructor order: Derived first, then Base.
Know the 5 types of inheritance: single, multiple, multilevel, hierarchical, hybrid
Private members are NEVER directly accessible in derived classes — use protected

practiceQuestions.question: If class B inherits from class A privately, what happens to A's public members in B?
options: They are not accessible at all
practiceQuestions.explanation: With private inheritance, all public and protected members of A become private in B. This means they're accessible inside B's methods but not from outside or in further derived classes.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the order of constructor calls in inheritance?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The base class constructor is called first (to initialize the base part), then the derived class constructor is called (to initialize the derived part). Think of it as building the foundation before the house.

practiceQuestions.question: Which access specifier allows members to be accessed in derived classes but not from outside?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Protected members are accessible within the class and in derived classes, but NOT from outside the class. This is specifically designed for inheritance scenarios.

lessons.title: Polymorphism — Function Overloading and Virtual Functions
lessons.overview: Polymorphism means 'many forms' — the same function name or operator can behave differently depending on the context. In C++, polymorphism is achieved through function overloading (compile-time), operator overloading (compile-time), and virtual functions (runtime). Runtime polymorphism uses a base class pointer to call derived class methods.
keyConcepts: Compile-time polymorphism: resolved at compile time — function overloading and operator overloading
Runtime polymorphism: resolved at runtime — virtual functions and overriding
Function Overloading: same function name, different parameter lists (number, type, or order)
Operator Overloading: redefine what an operator (+, -, [], etc.) does for user-defined types
Virtual Function: declared with 'virtual' keyword in base class, overridden in derived class
Override: derived class provides its own implementation of a virtual function
Base class pointer + virtual function = runtime polymorphism (dynamic dispatch)
Pure Virtual Function: virtual void func() = 0; — makes the class abstract (cannot be instantiated)
formulas: Function overloading: void print(int); void print(float); void print(string);

tables.title: Compile-time vs Runtime Polymorphism
tables.note: Runtime polymorphism uses a vtable (virtual table) to look up the correct function at runtime.

codeExamples.title: Runtime Polymorphism with Virtual Functions
codeExamples.explanation: Even though s1 and s2 are Shape pointers, the correct draw() and area() methods of Circle and Rectangle are called at runtime because they are declared virtual. This is runtime polymorphism. Shape is abstract (has a pure virtual function area()=0), so you can't create a Shape object directly.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the 'virtual' keyword in the base class — without it, the base class method is called even for derived objects
Not making the base class destructor virtual — when deleting through a base pointer, the derived destructor won't be called
Confusing overloading (same name, different params) with overriding (same name, same params, different class)
Trying to instantiate an abstract class (one with pure virtual functions)
examTips: Virtual functions enable runtime polymorphism — always use 'virtual' in the base class
Pure virtual function (= 0) makes the class abstract — cannot be instantiated
Function overloading is compile-time; virtual functions are runtime
Always make the base class destructor virtual if you use inheritance + dynamic allocation
Know the difference: overloading (same name, different params) vs overriding (same name, same params, derived class)

practiceQuestions.question: What keyword is used to achieve runtime polymorphism in C++?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The 'virtual' keyword tells the compiler to use dynamic dispatch (vtable lookup) at runtime. Without it, the base class method is called based on the pointer type, not the actual object type.

practiceQuestions.question: What is a pure virtual function?
options: A function declared with = 0, making the class abstract
A function that cannot be overridden
practiceQuestions.explanation: A pure virtual function is declared with '= 0' syntax: virtual void func() = 0;. It has no implementation in the base class and must be overridden in derived classes. A class with at least one pure virtual function is abstract and cannot be instantiated.

practiceQuestions.question: What is function overloading?
options: Redefining a function in a derived class
Having multiple functions with the same name but different parameters
Calling a function from another function
practiceQuestions.explanation: Function overloading is having multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists (different number, type, or order of parameters). The compiler decides which version to call based on the arguments. This is compile-time polymorphism.
